note: What a creature is, where behaviours/ holds what it does. A speed or a bite is argued about far more often than the code that reads it, and reads better in a diff as "the bear now hits for three" than as a changed literal four screens into a source file. The shape a creature is drawn as stays in the source, because a shape is read by looking at it rather than by being told.
The fields, once, here, because every file in this directory uses the same ones.

`scale` multiplies the whole rig. `speed` and `runSpeed` are tiles a second: the hero walks and runs at 5.5, so anything above that cannot be left behind and anything below it can. `herd` is the fewest and the most that turn up together. `behaviour` names the tree in behaviours/ that decides for this kind, unless a tree is filed under its own name, in which case that one wins. `timid` is whether it bolts from the hero.

`climb` is how far up a creature may step; leave it out and it gets the walker's STEP_LIMIT from behaviour.json, which is under the half-unit lip of a terrace and so makes one a wall. The hero's 0.56 clears exactly one terrace, which is what makes them an answer to anything that has no climb of its own.

`dangerous` is what one blow costs, out of the hero's ten hearts, and its absence means a creature that never attacks anybody. `blow` picks the shape it throws when it does; left out, anything with an arm punches and anything without bites. `hp` is what it takes to put down — leave it out and a blade passes straight through, which is a wight rather than an oversight. `owned` marks somebody's livestock, so killing it is rustling and the village finds out. `gold` is the purse, `drop` what is on the body and how often.

`altitude` is how high a flier holds itself above the ground. `palettes` are the colour sets one creature is painted from — a herd of cows is four different cows because there are four of these — and the parts of the rig index into whichever one they were dealt. `names` and `lines` are what it is called and what it says.

cow.note: Slow enough to be caught by anybody, and the hit points are only there so that it can be killed at all. What makes a cow expensive is `owned`: a farmer's cow is a rustling charge rather than a fight.
cow.label: Cow

sheep.note: The cow's argument with less of the animal: larger flocks, fewer hit points, and the same consequence for taking one.
sheep.label: Sheep

horse.note: Owned like the rest of the farm and the quickest thing on it — at a run it is barely short of the hero, which is most of the reason anybody wants to be sitting on one.
horse.label: Horse

deer.note: It runs at exactly the hero's pace, so a deer is never caught by chasing it. Meat off a deer is a matter of cutting it off, or of owning a bow.
deer.label: Deer

rabbit.note: One hit point and quick with it. Nothing about a rabbit is a fight; it is a thing you either catch or do not.
rabbit.label: Rabbit

fox.note: The one animal that is neither prey nor a threat: `timid` is false, so it does not run from you, and `dangerous` is absent, so it never means anything by watching.
fox.label: Fox

note: One bear, and it takes a beating and gives one.

It had a cow's hit points and a rat's bite, which made the largest animal in the world three swings of a stick and twenty-five gold: a payday, not a bad idea. Solitary, hitting for a fifth of a fresh hero and standing up to twenty points of stick, it now costs a beginner more than half of themselves; and it ambles at 0.8, so the answer is always allowed to be "no".
bear.label: Bear

camel.note: Desert livestock, and priced as the horse's opposite: as much animal to get through, none of the pace.
camel.label: Camel

lizard.note: No hit points, so a blade passes through it and there is nothing on it to take. Too small to be a fight and too small to be a meal — it is scenery that moves.
lizard.label: Lizard

frog.note: Scenery that moves, like the lizard, and for the same reason: nothing to kill and nothing to carry home.
frog.label: Frog

goat.note: The mountain's own livestock, and nobody's: it lives where no farm reaches, so `owned` is absent and killing one costs nothing but the walk.
goat.label: Goat

hare.note: The rabbit again, wearing snow. Faster, because there is nowhere on an open snowfield to hide instead.
hare.label: Snow Hare

wolf.note: One damage a bite is a tenth of a fresh hero, which is survivable one wolf at a time — and is exactly why they arrive in twos and fours. A pack is the first thing in the world that can actually finish you.
wolf.label: Wolf

elk.note: The snow's deer: heavier, slower to bolt, and worth more meat for the walk out.
elk.label: Elk
